items.title: OpenAI Reports GPT-6 Can Design Proteins, With Wet-Lab Binding Evidence
items.summary: On Nov 24 OpenAI published a preprint and blog post saying the GPT-6 family can design novel protein structures and amino-acid sequences using reasoning and general-purpose code, without calling specialized biology models to generate the designs. With research partner Onava, 35 of 322 minibinders built from GPT-6.2-designed structures showed evidence of binding across five targets; redesigned antibody fragments retained binding in 66-85% of tested cases. Specialized models still supplied sequences and helped select candidates for lab testing. OpenAI says predicting a complete protein structure from sequence remains a clear weakness (TM-score 0.38 versus 0.93 for ESMFold2), and that the results do not establish end-to-end zero-shot design. The research is a preprint, not peer reviewed.
items.impact: If general models can absorb natural-language design constraints normally handled by specialist tools, early drug-discovery workflows could become cheaper and more flexible. Two cautions: binding is not a working, safe therapy, and the dual-use biosecurity risk grows as these capabilities spread.

items.title: AWS Strands Releases Decider v2 Open-Weight Decision Models for AI Agents
items.summary: On Nov 23 the AWS-backed Strands Agents project released Decider v2, five open-weight decision models built on Google's Gemma 4 and spanning E2B to 31B parameters under an Apache 2.0 license. Instead of generating free text, a Decider scores supplied options in a single pass, aiming at agent jobs such as tool selection, request routing, guardrails and answer-quality checks. Trained on 17.5 million examples, the largest model averages 82.1 across six public text benchmarks versus 70.0 for the cited v1 comparator, with calibration error falling from 0.062 to 0.027. AWS reports that an earlier-generation Decider cut ticket-labelling costs by 98% on a large internal system. All benchmark and cost figures are vendor-reported, not independently verified.
items.impact: Small, cheap, bounded models could absorb the many routine judgments inside agents, cutting inference cost and making human-escalation thresholds measurable. Teams should still validate calibration and error rates on their own tasks before replacing a reasoning model in high-stakes flows.

items.title: Hex.pm Patches CVSS 10 RCE After Six Package Registry Servers Are Compromised
items.summary: Attackers exploited CVE-2026-129514, a maximum-severity remote-code-execution flaw, on Nov 23 to run operating-system commands on six production servers of Hex.pm, the registry used by Elixir and Erlang developers. The bug sat in an Erlang-term parser that ran before routing and authentication: a crafted __struct__ map caused error-handling code to call an attacker-chosen function. Load-balancer logs show 69 exploit requests in 13 minutes from two addresses. Maintainers put every server on a patched build within about 15 minutes, found no evidence any package was altered, and reset all sessions and access tokens. They could not rule out reads of email addresses, password hashes, two-factor secrets or private packages, and reported the incident to CISA, ENISA and Sweden's data protection authority.
items.impact: Any registry compromise is a supply-chain event, because a short window can still seed malicious releases. Users should change passwords, reset 2FA and fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm until a new signed client ships; self-hosted registries need the patch too.

items.title: Microsoft Confirms Azure API Management Flaw Was Exploited to Steal Cloud Secrets
items.summary: Microsoft issued a critical advisory after attackers raided Azure API Management (APIM) Classic instances for stored secrets and performed administrative operations. Exposure depended on instances not following Microsoft's network-security guidance, or storing secrets directly in APIM instead of referencing Azure Key Vault; APIM v2 was unaffected. Microsoft says it identified the issue on Nov 18 and automatically closed the access path on Nov 19, but acknowledges customers were exposed before that. Potentially accessed material includes named-value secrets, identity-provider and OpenID Connect client secrets, subscription keys and direct management-API tokens. Norway's National Security Authority linked the flaw to intrusions at energy firms Equinor and Skagerak Energi and warned that other sectors and countries are affected. The extent of exploitation remains unknown.
items.impact: Closing the access path does not un-steal credentials. Organizations should assume exposure, rotate every secret held in APIM and hunt for downstream use, especially in forgotten development and test instances that often lack monitoring.

items.title: 1Password Discloses Backend Breach Exposing Some Customer Account Records
items.summary: On Nov 25 password manager 1Password disclosed that it began investigating on Nov 19 after signs that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account. The intruder used that access to copy source code from private repositories, push malicious code to backend services and download account records for a subset of customers. Exposed fields include names, sign-in email addresses, account and user identifiers, creation and last-sign-in times, public keys, SRP parameters and tokens embedded in invitation, provisioning and recovery links. 1Password says customer vaults, the keys protecting them, recovery keys and its apps and browser extensions were not affected. It disabled the GitHub account, revoked stolen tokens, rotated credentials and lengthened emailed verification codes from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters.
items.impact: Zero-knowledge vault encryption did its job: no passwords or vault contents were taken. But names paired with real sign-in emails and recovery tokens create a strong phishing window, so customers should open the app or type the URL themselves rather than follow 1Password-themed messages.
